As such, establishing an escalation procedure contributes a major task in the preparation and planning stage.", "bbox": [ 189, 556, 875, 658 ], "page_idx": 29 }, { "type": "text", "text": "An escalation procedure will set out the points of contact (both internal and external), with corresponding contact information, at various levels for notification based on the type and severity of impact caused by the incident.", "bbox": [ 189, 677, 868, 730 ], "page_idx": 29 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Escalation procedures may be different for different kinds of incidents, in terms of the contact points and follow-up actions. Specific contact lists should be maintained to handle different kinds of incidents that involve different expertise or management decisions.", "bbox": [ 189, 751, 882, 816 ], "page_idx": 29 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Some recommendations on escalation procedure together with a sample escalation procedure are set out in Annex D for reference. A typical workflow on reporting and escalation of government security incidents is also illustrated in Annex E for reference.", "bbox": [ 189, 840, 863, 906 ], "page_idx": 29 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Detection and Reporting", "bbox": [ 675, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 29 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 115, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 29 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "25", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 29 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.2.3 Response procedures", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 114, 109, 394, 129 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Depending on different systems and management requirements, examples of incident handling procedures may include:", "bbox": [ 184, 152, 815, 185 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Assess the impact and damage of the incident.", "bbox": [ 186, 209, 603, 225 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Resume the system to normal operation in the shortest possible time.", "bbox": [ 186, 230, 784, 247 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Minimise the impact to other systems.", "bbox": [ 186, 252, 539, 268 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Avoid further incidents.", "bbox": [ 186, 272, 425, 287 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Identify the root cause of the incident.", "bbox": [ 186, 293, 537, 310 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Collect evidence to support subsequent case investigation.", "bbox": [ 186, 313, 699, 331 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Update policies and procedures as needed.", "bbox": [ 186, 335, 573, 353 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Some incidents may be too complicated or large in scale that it is difficult to address all issues at the same time. Defining priorities is essential to allow the personnel involved to focus on the most critical events first. The following are some suggested priorities to be focused on:", "bbox": [ 184, 375, 880, 442 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Protect human life and safety.", "bbox": [ 186, 466, 472, 482 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Protect critical resources.", "bbox": [ 186, 487, 435, 502 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Protect sensitive or important data which is costly when lost or damaged.", "bbox": [ 186, 507, 820, 524 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Prevent damage to systems with costly downtime and recovery cost.", "bbox": [ 186, 529, 781, 545 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Minimise disruption of service.", "bbox": [ 186, 549, 484, 565 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Protect public image of the B/D or the Government as a whole.", "bbox": [ 186, 570, 739, 588 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.2.4 Recovery Plan", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 607, 332, 626 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "An effective recovery plan is critical for restoring systems to normal operations after a security incident. The recovery plan should be comprehensive, well-documented, and include steps to ensure the security and integrity of the system upon restoration.", "bbox": [ 184, 645, 878, 697 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Detection and Reporting", "bbox": [ 675, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 115, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "26", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 878, 957 ], "page_idx": 30 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The recovery plan should cover:", "bbox": [ 191, 89, 460, 105 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• The procedures for damage assessment and identification of affected services.", "bbox": [ 189, 107, 857, 123 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• The prioritisation of system restoration and service resumption.", "bbox": [ 189, 124, 741, 141 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• The steps to securely re-install damaged or compromised components.", "bbox": [ 189, 142, 798, 158 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• The verification process to ensure systems are restored to a state of normalcy.", "bbox": [ 191, 159, 853, 175 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Communication protocols for notifying relevant parties about the status of recovery.", "bbox": [ 189, 177, 831, 210 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The recovery procedure should encompass the following steps:", "bbox": [ 191, 225, 709, 242 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Conduct a thorough damage assessment to determine the extent and impact of the incident.", "bbox": [ 191, 243, 860, 274 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Determine the order in which functions and services should be restored, prioritising essential services and those impacting the majority of users.", "bbox": [ 191, 277, 810, 310 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Re-install damaged or deleted files from a trusted source, ensuring the integrity and security of the software.", "bbox": [ 191, 311, 868, 343 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Resume functions/services in a controlled manner, starting with the most critical services.", "bbox": [ 191, 344, 877, 376 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Verify that the system has been restored to normal operations and that no traces of the security incident remain.", "bbox": [ 191, 378, 872, 411 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Inform all related parties about the resumption of system operations, ensuring that operators, administrators, and senior management are aware of the current status.", "bbox": [ 191, 412, 863, 461 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Turn off any services that are not essential to minimise the system’s attack surface.", "bbox": [ 191, 481, 830, 514 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Document all actions taken during the recovery process.", "bbox": [ 189, 516, 682, 533 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Section 9 below provides a reference model for dealing with security incidents, in particular containment, eradication, and recovery processes.", "bbox": [ 189, 548, 860, 583 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.2.5 Communication Plan", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 601, 394, 621 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Communication procedures with stakeholders and the general public should be established. Communication is essential to control the messaging surrounding the incident, including where, when, what and how this messaging is delivered. Internal communication is necessary for an effective response and recovery, and external communication is indispensable for safeguarding the government’s image. Uncontrolled communication about an incident can have serious consequences. Only duly mandated and prepared personnel should be allowed to communicate on behalf of B/Ds to tell what is necessary, at the best moment, and in the appropriate form.", "bbox": [ 189, 640, 873, 790 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "An effective communication plan should begin by identifying the key audiences that need to be informed during an incident. These typically include internal stakeholders such as users, management, and the incident response team and external stakeholders like citizens, partners, regulators, and the media. For each audience, the plan should designate specific messages, channels for communication, and the frequency with which updates should be provided.", "bbox": [ 189, 812, 880, 913 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Detection and Reporting", "bbox": [ 675, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "27", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 115, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 31 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The plan should detail the communication infrastructure, including primary and backup communication methods, to ensure uninterrupted information flow. This could involve emails, internal bulletins, press releases, social media, and press conferences. The infrastructure must be robust enough to handle the increased communication volume during a crisis.", "bbox": [ 189, 109, 852, 193 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Roles and responsibilities must be clearly defined within the communication plan. This includes appointing a spokesperson or a team of spokespersons trained in crisis communication who will deliver messages to the public and media. There should also be protocols for the approval and dissemination of messages to ensure consistency and accuracy.", "bbox": [ 189, 214, 878, 299 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The plan should also include pre-drafted templates for various scenarios to expedite communication. These templates can be quickly adapted to fit the specific details of an incident, ensuring a rapid response.", "bbox": [ 189, 321, 882, 370 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The communication plan must be flexible and adapt to the incident’s changing nature. It should include a feedback loop to assess the communication’s effectiveness and make necessary adjustments. After the incident is resolved, reviewing the communication process is essential to identify what worked well and what could be improved for future incidents. This review process ensures that the communication plan is a living document that evolves based on past experiences.", "bbox": [ 189, 392, 872, 494 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.2.6 Post-incident review procedures", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 516, 499, 535 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The post-incident review is an essential component of the security incident response plan. It thoroughly analyses the incident, its response, and the recovery steps. The post-incident review procedures should be methodical and documented, incorporating lessons learned to improve future response and prevention measures. The review should evaluate the security incident’s handling, identify successes and failures, and detail actions to improve future incident response capabilities. The review should encompass:", "bbox": [ 189, 557, 875, 674 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• The initial detection and reporting of the incident.", "bbox": [ 189, 696, 631, 714 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• The effectiveness of the response and containment strategies.", "bbox": [ 191, 718, 722, 734 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• The accuracy and efficiency of the communication plan execution.", "bbox": [ 191, 739, 766, 756 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• The adequacy of the recovery plan and its execution.", "bbox": [ 191, 760, 655, 777 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• The restoration of normal operations and services.", "bbox": [ 191, 781, 635, 797 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• The process of evidence preservation and its role in the analysis.", "bbox": [ 191, 802, 749, 819 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The review procedure should be structured as follows:", "bbox": [ 191, 841, 638, 859 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The review should be initiated after the recovery phase and normal operations are restored.", "bbox": [ 191, 863, 882, 895 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Detection and Reporting", "bbox": [ 675, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 115, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "28", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 32 }, { "type": "text", "text": "All documentation and logs related to the incident should be collected and reviewed to reconstruct the timeline and actions taken.", "bbox": [ 189, 89, 882, 123 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Evaluate the response performance against the established metrics and identify any deviations from the response plan.", "bbox": [ 189, 128, 880, 161 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Conduct meetings with the incident response team, management, and other relevant stakeholders to discuss the incident and gather feedback.", "bbox": [ 189, 165, 882, 198 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Prepare a comprehensive report that includes:", "bbox": [ 191, 203, 600, 219 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "o A summary of the incident and its impact.", "bbox": [ 228, 222, 606, 239 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "o The strengths and weaknesses of the response.", "bbox": [ 228, 242, 640, 259 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "o Recommendations for future improvement.", "bbox": [ 228, 262, 616, 279 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "o Actionable steps to address identified weaknesses.", "bbox": [ 228, 281, 673, 299 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "A meeting should be held to discuss the report findings, ensuring that all stakeholders have an understanding of the outcomes and the necessary improvements.", "bbox": [ 198, 303, 882, 354 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The incident response team shall be responsible for the following:", "bbox": [ 198, 375, 741, 393 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Tracking the implementation of improvements identified during the review.", "bbox": [ 198, 397, 847, 414 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Updating policies, procedures, and response plans as required.", "bbox": [ 198, 418, 739, 435 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Conducting training and awareness sessions to address the gaps identified.", "bbox": [ 198, 438, 836, 456 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Re-evaluating metrics and adjusting them to better measure future incident responses.", "bbox": [ 198, 460, 882, 494 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Records of all post-incident reviews should be maintained to inform future incident responses and compliance requirements. These records should be secure and accessible only to authorised personnel. The post-incident review process should be iterative, with each incident providing insights for continuous improvement in the security incident response plan.", "bbox": [ 189, 516, 884, 600 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.3 Planning of Training and Education", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 114, 621, 532, 643 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "B/Ds shall ensure all staff observe and follow the security incident response plan for information systems accordingly. Staff should be familiar with the procedures to handle the incident from incident reporting, identification, and taking the appropriate actions to recover the system to normal operation. Drills on incident handling should also be organised regularly for staff to practise the procedures. B/Ds shall also participate in security drills designated by DPO. After a drill is conducted, the result should be reviewed and recommendations should be proposed to improve the incident handling procedures where appropriate.", "bbox": [ 184, 657, 878, 791 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "In addition, sufficient training for system operation and support staff on security precaution knowledge is also important, in order to strengthen the security protection of the system or functional area, and reduce the chance that an incident may occur. As end users are often the first to notice that something is wrong, they should be encouraged to report anomalies or suspected breaches of security.", "bbox": [ 184, 812, 880, 897 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Detection and Reporting", "bbox": [ 675, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "29", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 115, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 33 }, { "type": "text", "text": "7. Detection and Reporting", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 108, 442, 128 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "7.1 Detection Measure", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 130, 374, 149 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "B/Ds should ensure detection and monitoring mechanism to detect security events is in place. B/Ds should detect and report the occurrence of an information security event aided by the following:", "bbox": [ 184, 173, 875, 224 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Alerts from network monitoring devices, such as firewalls, network flow analysis tools, or web filtering tools.", "bbox": [ 186, 247, 818, 280 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Alerts from security monitoring devices, such as intrusion detection systems, intrusion prevention systems, anti-malware solutions, log monitoring systems, or security information management systems.", "bbox": [ 186, 285, 862, 335 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Analysis of log information from devices, services, hosts, and various systems.", "bbox": [ 186, 338, 865, 356 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Reports from users or help desk.", "bbox": [ 186, 360, 492, 376 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "External notifications coming from outsiders such as threat intelligence platforms, other ISIRTs, telecommunication service providers, Internet service providers (ISPs), general public, media, or external service providers.", "bbox": [ 186, 380, 865, 431 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "ISIRT should maintain an inventory for all information security events of the B/D.", "bbox": [ 186, 453, 858, 470 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "7.2 Reporting", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 493, 290, 514 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "A staff should follow the reporting procedures to bring the security events to the attention of the ISIRT. It is essential that all staff are well aware of and have access to the report procedures for reporting different types of possible information security events. The following information should be the basis of reporting an information security event:", "bbox": [ 184, 536, 878, 619 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Date/time for detection", "bbox": [ 186, 643, 418, 658 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Systems affected", "bbox": [ 188, 664, 369, 680 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Observations", "bbox": [ 188, 686, 337, 700 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Contact information of the person who reports the security event", "bbox": [ 186, 706, 752, 722 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Detection and Reporting", "bbox": [ 675, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 115, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "30", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 878, 957 ], "page_idx": 34 }, { "type": "text", "text": "8. Assessment and Decision", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 89, 443, 108 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Upon discovery of suspicious activities, the information system's user, operator or administrator should follow the predefined reporting procedure to report the incident to the respective information system manager. A standard security incident report form may be used to collect information, and to support further investigation and analysis. On the other hand, monitoring tools, such as intrusion detection tools and system audit logs, can be used to aid in identifying unauthorised or abnormal activities.", "bbox": [ 184, 131, 877, 247 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "After abnormality has been detected, the respective information system manager should start to identify the incident, which involves the following steps:", "bbox": [ 184, 269, 845, 305 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Determine if an incident has occurred and perform a preliminary assessment.", "bbox": [ 186, 328, 850, 344 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Log the incident.", "bbox": [ 186, 349, 368, 366 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Obtain system snapshots, if necessary.", "bbox": [ 186, 369, 539, 387 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "To determine if an incident has occurred, B/Ds should consider the following circumstances, including but not be limited to:", "bbox": [ 186, 400, 818, 435 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• whether the concerned system is deployed in the Government;", "bbox": [ 186, 456, 744, 473 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• if the concerned system is deployed not in the Government,", "bbox": [ 186, 476, 724, 493 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(i) whether the system is being provided and maintained by the Government; and", "bbox": [ 186, 497, 872, 514 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(ii) whether the incident is caused by vulnerabilities of the system or factors not under the control of the Government; for example, the party who deployed the system has done something at fault or omitted doing something against the advice of the Government.", "bbox": [ 186, 516, 873, 583 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "For instance, a B/D discovers a vulnerability in its provided and maintained system which is deployed not in the Government. Subsequently, the B/D makes available patch for the vulnerability and informs the users who deployed the system to install the patch. If the users fail to do so and then the system deployed is hacked, this should normally not be regarded as a government security incident. It also excludes the case in which a security breach occurred on a smart phone installed with a mobile app with security patch already available but the user has failed to install the patch.", "bbox": [ 184, 605, 873, 739 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 667, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "31", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 115, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 35 }, { "type": "text", "text": "8.1 Assessment of Incident", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 89, 413, 108 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "text", "text": "First of all, the respective information system manager should determine whether or not an incident has actually occurred. However, it is often difficult to determine whether the abnormality found is a symptom of an incident. Some evidences may reveal that the abnormality is caused by something else, for example, hardware failures or user errors.", "bbox": [ 184, 131, 873, 215 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "text", "text": "To determine if an abnormality is a result of system problems or actual incidents, ISIRT should collect information about the detection of an information security event and seek any clarification from the person who reports the security event. Advice from GIRO-SO could be sought, when needed, if there are signs indicating the potential for an information security incident. Some typical indications of an incident that deserve special attention, typical security incidents as well as the criteria to be considered when determining the scope and impact of the incident are suggested in Annex F for reference.", "bbox": [ 184, 237, 867, 370 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "text", "text": "8.2 Escalation", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 392, 292, 411 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "text", "text": "After an event is identified to be an information security incident, the information system manager should then determine the type of the incident, and assess its scope, damage and impact in order to effectively deal with it. This initial analysis process plays a critical role in understanding the incident and formulating an appropriate response. By implementing a structured initial analysis process, we can ensure that the incident is thoroughly evaluated and that the necessary precautions and defensive measures are promptly taken. A standardised checklist that serves as a guide for gathering incident details and evaluating critical factors should be leveraged to aid in this process.", "bbox": [ 184, 430, 882, 581 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The checklist should integrate seamlessly into the escalation process when notifying the appropriate parties and escalating the incident to the appropriate level. When describing the incident during the escalation process, the following information is suggested to be included:", "bbox": [ 184, 601, 875, 670 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "text", "text": "A. Incident Details: Capture the date and time of the incident, along with a brief summary description. This information will provide a snapshot of the incident's timeline and nature.", "bbox": [ 174, 692, 855, 741 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "text", "text": "1. Date and Time: Record the exact date and time when the incident occurred or was first detected. This timestamp will serve as a reference point for tracking the incident's progression and response timeline.", "bbox": [ 218, 757, 863, 806 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "text", "text": "2. Incident Summary: Provide a concise description of the incident. Include relevant details such as the nature of the incident (e.g., security breach, system outage, data loss), the affected system(s), and any initial observations or symptoms. This summary will help stakeholders quickly grasp the incident's context and initiate appropriate response actions.", "bbox": [ 216, 806, 877, 857 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 668, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 942, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "32", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 36 }, { "type": "text", "text": "", "bbox": [ 245, 89, 813, 122 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "3. Incident Classification: Classify the incident based on predefined categories or severity levels. Common classifications may include security incidents, technical failures, human errors, or natural disasters. Assigning a classification to the incident aids in prioritising response efforts and allocating resources effectively.", "bbox": [ 216, 122, 877, 204 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "4. Incident Source: Identify the source or origin of the incident, if known. This could be a specific event, action, or external factor that triggered the incident. Understanding the incident source can provide valuable insights into potential causes and assist in identifying preventive measures.", "bbox": [ 216, 204, 880, 269 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "5. Reporting Party: Note the individual or team that reported the incident. Include their contact information for further communication or clarification, if necessary. This information helps establish a direct line of communication with the reporting party for additional incident details or updates.", "bbox": [ 216, 269, 873, 335 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6. Notification and Escalation: Document any initial notifications or escalations made regarding the incident. Include the individuals or teams notified, the communication channels used, and the time of notification. This information can help ensure that the incident response process is properly initiated and communicated to the relevant stakeholders.", "bbox": [ 216, 336, 877, 417 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "i. Informed Parties: Document which parties were informed about the incident, including HKPF, PCPD, and media if relevant.", "bbox": [ 268, 417, 852, 450 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "ii. Action Taken: Record the immediate actions taken following the incident. This could include isolation of the affected system, initiation of forensics, or activation of a crisis management team.", "bbox": [ 265, 450, 875, 500 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "B. System Information: Include details about the affected system(s) and their respective owners. If multiple departments co-own a system, note the relevant departments involved. Understanding ownership is vital for effective communication and collaboration.", "bbox": [ 174, 516, 843, 582 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "1. System Owner Contact Information: Provide a sub-field to capture the contact details (name, email, phone number) of the system owner or the person responsible for the affected system. This information will facilitate communication and coordination during the incident response.", "bbox": [ 203, 598, 882, 665 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "2. System Criticality: The system criticality helps determine the level of impact and urgency associated with the incident. Consider the following factors when assessing system criticality:", "bbox": [ 203, 680, 873, 730 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "2.1. System Tiering: System tier(s) assigned to each affected system.", "bbox": [ 235, 745, 811, 762 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "2.2. Business Impact: Evaluate the impact that the loss or degradation of the affected system would have on critical business operations. Consider factors such as revenue generation, user service, regulatory compliance, and reputation.", "bbox": [ 235, 762, 873, 826 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "2.3. Availability Requirements: Determine the expected level of system availability based on business and operational needs. Consider factors such as service level agreements (SLAs), uptime requirements, and the system's role in supporting time-sensitive processes.", "bbox": [ 235, 827, 855, 862 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 667, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "33", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 37 }, { "type": "text", "text": "", "bbox": [ 280, 89, 862, 122 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "2.4. Data Sensitivity: Assess the sensitivity and confidentiality of the data processed, stored, or transmitted by the affected system.", "bbox": [ 235, 122, 855, 154 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "2.5. Recovery Time Objectives (RTO): The RTO represents the maximum tolerable duration for restoring the system to full functionality after an incident. It helps prioritise response efforts and allocate resources effectively.", "bbox": [ 235, 155, 858, 219 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "2.6. Recovery Point Objectives (RPO): The RPO represents the maximum tolerable amount of data that could be lost during recovery. It helps establish backup and data recovery strategies to minimise potential data loss.", "bbox": [ 235, 221, 868, 286 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "3. System Description: Provide an overview of the system impacted by the incident. Include details such as the purpose of the system/application, its primary functionalities, and the role it plays in supporting business processes. This description will help stakeholders understand the importance of the application and its relevance to the B/D's operations.", "bbox": [ 206, 302, 870, 386 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "3.1. Workflow Overview: Describe the typical workflow or process flow within the system. Identify the key steps, actions, or interactions involved in using the application to achieve specific outcomes. This overview will provide a high-level understanding of how the application is used and its critical paths.", "bbox": [ 231, 400, 873, 482 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "3.2. Functionalities Affected: Identify the specific functionalities or features of the system that have been impacted by the incident. Describe the extent to which these functionalities are affected and the potential consequences of their unavailability or degradation. Understanding the impacted functionalities will help assess the severity of the incident and prioritise response actions.", "bbox": [ 233, 483, 873, 581 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "3.3. System Dependencies: Identify and document any dependencies that the affected system has on other systems/applications or services. This can include databases, APIs, network connections, or third-party integrations. Understanding these dependencies is crucial for assessing the potential impact of the incident on interconnected systems.", "bbox": [ 233, 581, 875, 663 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "3.4. Interactions with Users: Describe how users interact with the system. This can include user interfaces, input mechanisms, or communication channels. Understanding the user interactions will help assess the impact of the incident on user experience, productivity, and user satisfaction.", "bbox": [ 233, 664, 877, 731 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "4. System Documentation: Include a sub-field to note the availability of system documentation, such as user manuals, or architecture diagrams. This information will assist the incident response team in gaining a comprehensive understanding of the system's structure and functionalities.", "bbox": [ 205, 745, 872, 813 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "4.1. User Manuals: Document the availability of user manuals or guides associated with the affected system. These manuals provide detailed instructions on the system's setup, configuration, and operation. Note whether the manuals are readily accessible and if they cover relevant aspects of the system that are impacted by the incident. Having user manuals at hand helps the incident response team understand the intended use of the system, its features, and any specific configuration requirements.", "bbox": [ 235, 827, 848, 912 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 667, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "34", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 38 }, { "type": "text", "text": "", "bbox": [ 280, 89, 858, 139 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "text", "text": "4.2. Architecture Diagrams: Document the availability of architecture diagrams that depict the affected system's overall design and integration with other systems or components. Architecture diagrams provide insights into the system's modules, interfaces, and dependencies. Indicate whether architecture diagrams are accessible and if they accurately represent the current state of the system. Understanding the system's architecture helps in identifying potential weaknesses, assessing the impact of the incident on the system's functionalities, and planning an effective response.", "bbox": [ 235, 139, 880, 285 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "text", "text": "4.3. Backup and Recovery Procedures: Attach the backup and recovery procedures in place for the affected system. Include details such as backup frequency, storage location, and the availability of recent backups. This information will be valuable for assessing the recovery options and planning the restoration process.", "bbox": [ 236, 286, 852, 368 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "text", "text": "4.4. Other Relevant Documentation: Consider any additional documentation that may be relevant to the affected system. This could include system specifications, configuration guides, security policies, or any other documentation that provides insights into the system's structure, configuration, or security controls. Note the availability and accessibility of such documentation. Additional documentation enhances the incident response team's understanding of the system and assists in making informed decisions throughout the investigation and mitigation process.", "bbox": [ 235, 368, 880, 501 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "text", "text": "5. System Configuration: Include a sub-field to document the configuration details of the affected system, such as hardware specifications, software versions, and installed patches. This information will help in understanding the system's vulnerabilities and potential areas of compromise.", "bbox": [ 206, 516, 882, 583 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "text", "text": "5.1. Hardware Specifications: Document the hardware specifications of the affected system. This includes details such as the processor type and speed, amount of RAM, storage capacity, and any other relevant hardware components. Understanding the hardware specifications helps in assessing the system's capabilities, performance, and potential impact on incident response activities.", "bbox": [ 235, 598, 872, 696 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "text", "text": "5.2. Software Versions: Identify and document the software versions installed on the affected system. This includes the operating system, applications, frameworks, libraries, and any other software components. Specify the exact version numbers to provide precise information. Knowing the software versions helps in identifying known vulnerabilities, security patches, and potential areas of compromise.", "bbox": [ 235, 696, 870, 795 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "text", "text": "5.3. Installed Patches: Document the installed patches and updates on the affected system. This includes operating system patches, application updates, firmware updates, and any other relevant patches that have been applied. Specify the patch names, version numbers, and dates of installation. Understanding the patch status helps in assessing the", "bbox": [ 236, 795, 878, 878 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 667, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 942, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "35", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 39 }, { "type": "text", "text": "system's resilience to known vulnerabilities and determining if any missing patches could have contributed to the incident.", "bbox": [ 280, 89, 830, 122 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "text", "text": "5.4. Configuration Changes: Document any recent configuration changes made to the affected system. This includes changes to firewall rules, user privileges, network settings, or any other relevant configuration modifications. Specify the nature of the changes, when they were made, and the individuals responsible. Tracking configuration changes helps in identifying potential misconfigurations, unauthorised modifications, or policy violations that may have contributed to the incident.", "bbox": [ 235, 123, 878, 239 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6. Network Diagram: Document the internal IP addresses associated with the incident and provide a network topology relevant to the incident. This will assist in identifying potential attack vectors and understanding the incident's scope.", "bbox": [ 206, 253, 860, 321 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.1. Network Topology Overview: Provide an overview of the network topology relevant to the incident. This includes the layout and structure of the network infrastructure, including routers, switches, firewalls, and other network devices. Describe how different components are interconnected and the overall architecture of the network.", "bbox": [ 235, 335, 868, 417 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.2. Internal IP Addresses: Document the internal IP addresses associated with the incident. This includes the IP addresses of the affected systems, servers, and network devices. By noting these IP addresses, you can identify the specific components involved in the incident and track their connectivity within the network.", "bbox": [ 235, 417, 873, 499 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.3. Subnet Information: Identify the subnets or network segments relevant to the incident. This includes the range of IP addresses associated with each subnet and any relevant subnet masks. Understanding the subnet structure will help in analyzing network traffic patterns and potential areas of vulnerability.", "bbox": [ 236, 499, 868, 581 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.4. Network Device Configuration: Document the configuration details of network devices involved in the incident, such as routers, switches, firewalls, and intrusion detection systems. Include relevant information such as device models, firmware versions, and any specific configurations or rules that may impact the incident.", "bbox": [ 236, 581, 867, 663 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.5. Attack Vectors: Analyse the network diagram to identify potential attack vectors or paths that could be exploited by an attacker. This includes examining the connectivity between systems, access control mechanisms, and potential security weaknesses in the network infrastructure. By identifying the possible attack vectors, you can assess the incident's scope and potential impact on the network.", "bbox": [ 236, 663, 877, 762 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "text", "text": "6.6. Incident Scope: Based on the network diagram, assess the scope of the incident in terms of the affected network segments, systems, and services. Determine the extent to which the incident has spread within the network and identify any critical assets or sensitive areas that may be at risk. This assessment will help prioritise response actions and containment efforts.", "bbox": [ 236, 762, 878, 829 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 667, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 942, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "36", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 878, 957 ], "page_idx": 40 }, { "type": "text", "text": "", "bbox": [ 280, 89, 806, 122 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "text", "text": "C. Indicators of Compromise (IoCs): List any impacted IP addresses, hostnames, and usernames related to the incident. Identify suspicious files or processes and any evidence of unauthorised access or activities.", "bbox": [ 168, 139, 878, 189 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "text", "text": "1. Impacted IP Addresses: Identify and list the IP addresses that have been impacted or associated with the incident. This includes both internal and external IP addresses that are relevant to the investigation. Documenting impacted IP addresses helps in tracking the source and destination of network traffic, identifying potential attack vectors, and understanding the scope of the incident.", "bbox": [ 228, 204, 867, 302 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "text", "text": "2. Impacted Hostnames: Document any hostnames or domain names that have been impacted by the incident. This could include compromised websites, unauthorised subdomains, or unusual DNS resolution patterns. Listing impacted hostnames provides insights into potential areas of compromise and indicates which systems or services may have been targeted.", "bbox": [ 228, 303, 852, 400 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "text", "text": "3. Impacted Usernames: Identify any usernames or accounts that have been affected or compromised during the incident. This includes user accounts associated with the impacted systems, applications, or services. Documenting impacted usernames helps in tracking unauthorised access, identifying potential insider threats, and assessing the extent of the compromise.", "bbox": [ 228, 400, 862, 499 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "text", "text": "4. Suspicious Files or Processes: Document any suspicious files or processes discovered during the investigation. This includes malware, malicious scripts, unauthorised executables, or any other files or processes that raise suspicion. Provide details such as file names, file locations, and associated process names, if applicable. Identifying suspicious files or processes helps in understanding the nature of the incident, detecting potential malware infections, and initiating appropriate response actions.", "bbox": [ 228, 500, 875, 614 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "text", "text": "5. Evidence of Unauthorised Access or Activities: Document any evidence or indicators that suggest unauthorised access or malicious activities. This could include log entries, timestamps, unusual network traffic patterns, or any other anomalies observed during the investigation. Capturing evidence of unauthorised access or activities helps in understanding the attacker's techniques, identifying potential data breaches, and mitigating further risks.", "bbox": [ 228, 614, 878, 715 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "text", "text": "D. Remarks: In this section, include supporting details for each indicator of compromise. Explain why the indicators are considered a compromise and indicate the confidence level. Additionally, note any additional observations or information relevant to the incident.", "bbox": [ 168, 728, 878, 795 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "text", "text": "1. Indicator of Compromise (IoCs) Details: For each identified indicator of compromise (IP addresses, hostnames, usernames, suspicious files or processes, evidence of unauthorised access or activities), provide supporting details explaining why they are considered a compromise. Include specific observations, behaviours, or characteristics that led to their inclusion as", "bbox": [ 216, 810, 872, 895 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 667, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "37", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 41 }, { "type": "text", "text": "indicators. This can include log entries, network traffic analysis, system logs, or any other evidence collected during the investigation.", "bbox": [ 245, 89, 878, 122 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "text", "text": "2. Rationale for Compromise: Explain the rationale behind considering each indicator as a compromise. Describe the potential impact or risk associated with the indicator and how it aligns with known attack patterns, vulnerabilities, or malicious activities. This rationale will provide context and justification for the inclusion of each indicator as a compromise.", "bbox": [ 216, 122, 858, 204 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "text", "text": "3. Confidence Level: Indicate the confidence level associated with each indicator of compromise. This can range from low to high, reflecting the level of certainty in the assessment. Consider factors such as the quality of evidence, reliability of sources, and the expertise of the investigators. Assigning a confidence level helps in prioritising response actions and allocating resources appropriately.", "bbox": [ 216, 204, 858, 303 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "text", "text": "4. Additional Observations: Note any additional observations or information that are relevant to the incident but may not fit under specific indicators of compromise. This can include unusual system behaviours, findings from vulnerability assessments, or any other insights that may help in understanding the incident or its potential impact. These additional observations provide valuable context and contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the incident.", "bbox": [ 216, 303, 857, 418 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The information provided during the escalation process should be clear, concise, accurate and factual. It is imperative that B/Ds maintain constant availability of system information/documentation to support the veracity and completeness of the communication. Providing inaccurate, misleading or incomplete information may hinder the response process or may even worsen the situation. B/Ds should also consider whether some sensitive information could be given to external parties or not.", "bbox": [ 184, 436, 862, 552 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The manager of the respective information system, with the Incident Response Manager of the ISIRT as the overall coordinator, should notify the appropriate parties and escalate the incident to the appropriate level following the predefined escalation procedure.", "bbox": [ 184, 575, 848, 643 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "text", "text": "If a B/D confirms that an incident occurs, the relevant ISIRT Commander should report the incident to GIRO-SO within 60 minutes after the incident is first identified. Reporting an incident does not mark the end of ISIRT responsibilities. ISIRT are expected to remain available and actively engaged. Leaving work immediately after reporting an incident may result in delays or gaps in the incident response process, compromising ISIRT's ability to safeguard the B/D.", "bbox": [ 184, 664, 863, 766 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "text", "text": "For purposes of recording and co-ordination on handling of the incident, the ISIRT Commander should also complete the initial analysis and provide a Preliminary Information Security Incident Report (see Annex C.2) for reporting of information security incidents including, but not be limited to, the following categories (please refer to Annex F for further description) to the GIRO-SO.", "bbox": [ 184, 787, 865, 870 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Abuse of information systems.", "bbox": [ 191, 894, 477, 910 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 667, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "38", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 42 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Compromise of information systems or data assets.", "bbox": [ 191, 90, 643, 107 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Denial of service attack (including the central or departmental Internet gateway, email systems, the government websites and/or systems delivering electronic services to the public).", "bbox": [ 191, 111, 875, 160 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Leaking of classified data in electronic form.", "bbox": [ 191, 165, 593, 181 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Loss of mobile devices or removable media that contain classified data.", "bbox": [ 191, 185, 806, 203 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Masquerading.", "bbox": [ 191, 206, 351, 224 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Massive malware infection.", "bbox": [ 191, 228, 453, 243 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Ransomware.", "bbox": [ 191, 249, 341, 265 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Website defacement.", "bbox": [ 191, 269, 398, 286 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Incidents that are not security related (listed below) are not required to report to the GIRO-SO. Instead, the prevailing standards and procedures on system administration and operation should be followed.", "bbox": [ 184, 310, 867, 360 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• System affected by natural disasters, e.g. typhoon, flooding, fire, etc.", "bbox": [ 191, 384, 784, 401 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Hardware or software problem.", "bbox": [ 191, 405, 484, 420 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Data/communication line failure.", "bbox": [ 191, 425, 497, 442 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Power disruption.", "bbox": [ 191, 447, 373, 463 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Scheduled system downtime or maintenance slot.", "bbox": [ 191, 467, 630, 483 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• System failure due to administration/operation error.", "bbox": [ 191, 488, 655, 505 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Loss or destruction of classified data due to system or human error.", "bbox": [ 191, 510, 773, 526 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Fraudulent emails or websites not affecting government systems and data.", "bbox": [ 191, 530, 826, 548 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "In case of incident with major impact to government services and/or image, the GIRO-SO will closely monitor the development with ISIRT Commander. If the incident is a potential multiple point attack targeting at the Government as a whole, the Standing Office will immediately notify GIRO for information and necessary action.", "bbox": [ 184, 570, 867, 653 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "In handling an event of data breach, B/D may consider to take remedial steps as below:", "bbox": [ 186, 675, 838, 708 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Immediate gathering of essential information related to the breach.", "bbox": [ 191, 713, 768, 731 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Adopting appropriate measures to contain the breach.", "bbox": [ 191, 734, 662, 751 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Assessing the risk of harm.", "bbox": [ 191, 756, 448, 772 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Considering the giving of data breach notification.", "bbox": [ 191, 776, 636, 794 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "If personal data is involved in a security incident, B/D should report the case to PCPD as soon as possible by using the data breach notification form available at PCPD’s web site", "bbox": [ 184, 816, 845, 865 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(https://www.pcpd.org.hk/english/resources\\_centre/publications/forms/files/DBN\\_e. pdf). The data breach notification form can also be submitted online through PCPD’s website", "bbox": [ 184, 865, 877, 915 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 667, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "39", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 115, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 43 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(https://www.pcpd.org.hk/english/enforcement/data\\_breach\\_notification/dbn\\_form.h tml).", "bbox": [ 186, 89, 878, 123 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "In addition, B/Ds may refer to the “Guidance on Data Breach Handling and Data Breach Notifications” issued by PCPD.", "bbox": [ 186, 145, 852, 179 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(https://www.pcpd.org.hk/english/resources\\_centre/publications/files/guidance\\_note \\_dbn\\_e.pdf)", "bbox": [ 186, 181, 875, 217 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "B/Ds should also notify affected individuals as far as practicable. Justifiable exception on reporting needs to be approved by the Head of B/D.", "bbox": [ 186, 237, 813, 273 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau of HKPF should be contacted if a B/D suspects a computer crime has been committed. Advice and endorsement from the senior management of the ISIRT should be sought along with the initial analysis completion before reporting the case to HKPF. In addition, for any security incident reported to HKPF or PCPD, the GIRO-SO should also be notified for central recording and coordination support.", "bbox": [ 184, 294, 877, 395 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Please refer to Annex D for a sample escalation procedure and other related information about security incident escalation. A typical workflow on reporting and escalation of government security incidents is illustrated in Annex E for reference.", "bbox": [ 184, 417, 877, 468 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "8.3 Log the Incident", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 486, 351, 506 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "All security incidents, actions taken and the corresponding results shall be recorded. The records should be stored securely with cryptography, locks or access control. This can facilitate incident identification, assessment, and provide evidence for prosecution and other useful information for subsequent stages of incident handling. Logging should be carried out throughout the whole security incident response process. An incident reference number may be assigned to each incident to facilitate follow-up and tracing during the whole incident handling process.", "bbox": [ 184, 527, 878, 646 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "As a minimum requirement, the following information shall be logged:", "bbox": [ 186, 665, 768, 684 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• System events and other relevant information, such as audit logs.", "bbox": [ 191, 707, 756, 725 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• All actions taken, including the date, time and personnel involved.", "bbox": [ 191, 728, 764, 745 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• All external correspondence, including the date, time, content and parties involved.", "bbox": [ 191, 750, 820, 782 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 667, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "40", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 878, 957 ], "page_idx": 44 }, { "type": "text", "text": "8.4 Obtain System Snapshot", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 89, 426, 109 ], "page_idx": 45 }, { "type": "text", "text": "A snapshot of the compromised system should be obtained as soon as suspicious activities are detected, and as far as technically and operationally feasible. This can prevent the attacker from destroying the evidence and support subsequent case investigation, such as forensic evidence collection. The snapshot of the system may include the following items:", "bbox": [ 184, 131, 873, 215 ], "page_idx": 45 }, { "type": "text", "text": "System log files such as server log, network log, firewall/router log, access log, etc.", "bbox": [ 191, 239, 870, 271 ], "page_idx": 45 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Information of active system login or network connection, and corresponding process status.", "bbox": [ 191, 275, 857, 310 ], "page_idx": 45 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• An image of the compromised system built for investigation purpose and as evidence for subsequent follow-up action.", "bbox": [ 191, 312, 842, 347 ], "page_idx": 45 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Assessment and Decision", "bbox": [ 667, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 45 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 45 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "41", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 875, 957 ], "page_idx": 45 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Response to Security Incident", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 114, 89, 494, 110 ], "page_idx": 46 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Response to security incident involves developing procedure to evaluate incidents and to respond in order to restore affected system components and services as soon as possible. The procedure is broadly categorised into three stages: Containment, Eradication and Recovery as shown in Figure 9.1 below. Understanding the activities of each stage can facilitate the development of an effective security incident response procedure.", "bbox": [ 184, 131, 865, 233 ], "page_idx": 46 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The response procedure may not strictly follow the order of the three stages, which has to be customised to meet practical needs.", "bbox": [ 184, 253, 865, 288 ], "page_idx": 46 }, { "type": "image", "img_path": "images/06e25068fd0ee238253a92b98bdfe2a239504b1000413854ea04598a94f71381.jpg", "image_caption": [ "Figure 9.1 Major Stages in Security Incident Response" ], "image_footnote": [], "bbox": [ 336, 306, 742, 630 ], "page_idx": 46 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Response to Security Incident", "bbox": [ 631, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 46 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 46 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "42", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 46 }, { "type": "text", "text": "9.1 Containment", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 89, 317, 108 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The first stage of response to incidents is containment. The purpose of containment is to limit the scope, magnitude and impact of an incident. There exist some incidents, like malware infection, which can spread rapidly and cause extensive damages. Hence, B/Ds should limit the extent of an incident before it causes further damages.", "bbox": [ 184, 131, 877, 216 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Strategies and procedures for responding to different incidents with different resources should be predetermined and stated clearly in the security incident response procedure. For critical action, one may also need to seek management advice and approval from the ISIRT (which may also need to consult the GIRO if necessary).", "bbox": [ 184, 234, 857, 317 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Activities in this stage may include:", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 188, 340, 484, 356 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Conducting impact assessment of the incident on data and information system involved to confirm if the data or service has already been damaged by or infected in the incident.", "bbox": [ 191, 380, 860, 430 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Protecting classified or critical information and system. For instance, move the critical information to other media (or other systems) which are separated from the compromised system or network.", "bbox": [ 191, 435, 870, 483 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Deciding on the operation status of the compromised system.", "bbox": [ 191, 488, 722, 505 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Building an image of the compromised system for investigation purpose and as evidence for subsequent follow-up action.", "bbox": [ 191, 510, 870, 542 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Keeping a record of all actions taken during this stage.", "bbox": [ 191, 546, 670, 563 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Checking any systems associated with the compromised system through shared network-based services or through any trusting relationship.", "bbox": [ 191, 567, 870, 601 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "ISIRT should conduct review periodically to determine if the incident is under control. If it is not under control or it is going to have a severe impact on the B/D’s core services, follow the predefined escalation procedures for crisis management.", "bbox": [ 184, 623, 870, 675 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Response to Security Incident", "bbox": [ 631, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "43", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 47 }, { "type": "text", "text": "9.1.1 Operation Status of the Compromised System", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 114, 89, 626, 109 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "text", "text": "One of the important decisions to be made is whether to continue or suspend the operation and service of the compromised system. This will very much depend on the type and severity of the incident, the system requirement and the impact on public service and the image of the B/D and the Government as a whole, as well as the predefined goals and priorities in the incident response plan of the system.", "bbox": [ 184, 131, 865, 216 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Actions to be taken may include:", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 186, 234, 460, 252 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Shutting down or isolating the compromised computer or system temporarily to prevent further damage to other interconnected systems, in particular for incidents that will spread rapidly, for computers with sensitive information, or to prevent the compromised system from being used to launch attack on other connected systems.", "bbox": [ 191, 275, 872, 356 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Stopping operation of the compromised information system.", "bbox": [ 193, 362, 715, 379 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Disabling some of the system's functions.", "bbox": [ 193, 382, 566, 399 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Removing user access or login to the system.", "bbox": [ 193, 404, 593, 420 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Continuing the operation to collect evidence for the incident. This may only be applied to Tier 1 information systems that could accept some risks in service interruption or data damage, and it must be handled with extreme care and under close monitoring.", "bbox": [ 191, 424, 882, 491 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Response to Security Incident", "bbox": [ 631, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "44", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 48 }, { "type": "text", "text": "9.2 Eradication", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 89, 304, 108 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The next task following containment is eradication. Eradicating an incident is to remove the cause of the incident from the system, such as removing a malware from the infected system and media.", "bbox": [ 184, 131, 875, 181 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Prior to removing any files or stopping/killing any processes, it is advisable to collect all the necessary information, including all the log files, active network connections and process status information. It helps to collect evidence for subsequent investigation, which may be deleted or reset during system clean up.", "bbox": [ 184, 204, 842, 273 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "9.2.1 Possible Actions for Incident Eradication", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 114, 290, 571, 310 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "During the eradication stage, the following actions may need to be performed depending on the type and nature of the incidents as well as the system requirement:", "bbox": [ 184, 332, 873, 368 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Stop or kill all processes created or activated by hacker to stop the damage and force the hacker out.", "bbox": [ 191, 391, 867, 423 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Delete all files created by the hacker. System operators should archive the files before deletion for the purpose of case investigation.", "bbox": [ 191, 428, 872, 461 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Eliminate all the backdoors and malicious programs installed by the hacker.", "bbox": [ 191, 464, 842, 482 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Apply patches and fixes to vulnerabilities found on all operating systems, servers, network devices, etc. Test the system thoroughly before restoring it to normal operation.", "bbox": [ 191, 486, 867, 536 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Correct any improper settings in the system and network, e.g. mis-configuration in firewall and router.", "bbox": [ 191, 541, 875, 573 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "In case of a malware incident, follow the advices of anti-malware tool vendor to inoculate or remove the malware from all infected systems and media as appropriate.", "bbox": [ 191, 577, 875, 627 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Provide assurance that the backups are clean to prevent the system from being re-infected at a later stage when system recovery from backup is needed.", "bbox": [ 191, 631, 862, 664 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Make use of some other security tools to assist in the eradication process, for instance, security scanning tools to detect any intrusion, and apply the recommended solution. These tools should be kept up-to-date with the latest detection patterns.", "bbox": [ 191, 669, 853, 734 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Update the access passwords of all login accounts that may have been accessed by the hacker.", "bbox": [ 191, 739, 870, 771 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "In some cases, the supporting staff may need to reformat all the infected media and reinstall the system and data from backup, especially when they are not certain about the extent of the damage in a Tier 2 or above information system or it is difficult to completely clean up the system.", "bbox": [ 191, 776, 867, 843 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Keep a record of all actions performed.", "bbox": [ 191, 846, 546, 864 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Response to Security Incident", "bbox": [ 631, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 115, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "45", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 49 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The above are only examples of commonly adopted actions during security incidents. Eradication actions may vary depending on the nature of the incident and its impact on the systems affected. On some occasions, the B/D may need to seek advice from external parties, such as HKPF, PCPD and/or the external service providers, and to make reference to other B/Ds with similar incident handling experience. Management advice and coordination support from the ISIRT and the GIRO should be sought accordingly.", "bbox": [ 184, 89, 873, 205 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "9.3 Recovery", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 240, 285, 260 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The last stage in incident response is recovery. The purpose of this stage is to restore the system to its normal operation. Examples of tasks include:", "bbox": [ 186, 282, 823, 317 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Perform damage assessment.", "bbox": [ 191, 341, 463, 357 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Re-install the deleted/damaged files or the whole system, whenever required, from the trusted source.", "bbox": [ 191, 361, 852, 394 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Bring up function/service by stages, in a controlled manner, and in order of demand, e.g. the most essential services or those serving the majority may resume first.", "bbox": [ 191, 398, 840, 448 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Verify that the restoring operation was successful and the system is back to its normal operation.", "bbox": [ 191, 453, 862, 486 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Prior notification to all related parties on resumption of system operation, e.g. operators, administrators, senior management, and other parties involved in the escalation procedure.", "bbox": [ 191, 489, 868, 539 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Disable unnecessary services.", "bbox": [ 193, 544, 470, 560 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Keep a record of all actions performed.", "bbox": [ 193, 564, 546, 582 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Prior to restoring the system to normal operation, one important action is to conduct a pre-production security assessment to ensure that the compromised system and its related components are secured. It may involve the use of security scanning tools to confirm that the problem source of the incident is cleared, as well as to reveal any other possible security loopholes in the system. The assessment may focus in a particular area, or may cover the entire system, depending on the severity of the incident and the service level requirement of the system.", "bbox": [ 184, 601, 873, 718 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Approval from the senior management in the ISIRT shall be obtained for all recovery actions to be conducted, and if considered necessary, support and advice from the GIRO may also be sought.", "bbox": [ 186, 739, 855, 790 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Response to Security Incident", "bbox": [ 631, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 117, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "46", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 878, 957 ], "page_idx": 50 }, { "type": "text", "text": "10. Post-Incident Actions", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 115, 89, 411, 108 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Restoring a system to normal operation does not mark the end of a security incident handling process. It is also important to perform the necessary follow-up actions. Actions may include evaluation of the damage caused, system refinement to prevent recurrence of the incident, security policies and procedures update, and case investigation for subsequent prosecution.", "bbox": [ 184, 131, 875, 216 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Follow-up actions can lead to the following:", "bbox": [ 186, 236, 551, 255 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Improve incident response procedure.", "bbox": [ 191, 278, 534, 296 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Improve security measures to protect the system against future attacks.", "bbox": [ 191, 299, 801, 317 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Prosecute those who have breached the law.", "bbox": [ 191, 321, 586, 337 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Help others to familiarise with security incident response process.", "bbox": [ 191, 342, 763, 359 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Help to educate those parties involved about the experience learnt.", "bbox": [ 191, 361, 766, 380 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Follow-up actions include:", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 186, 401, 410, 419 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Post-incident analysis.", "bbox": [ 191, 443, 411, 460 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Post-incident report.", "bbox": [ 193, 464, 394, 481 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Security assessment.", "bbox": [ 193, 486, 396, 501 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Review existing protection.", "bbox": [ 191, 506, 452, 523 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Investigation and prosecution.", "bbox": [ 191, 526, 473, 544 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "10.1 Post-Incident Analysis", "text_level": 2, "bbox": [ 117, 567, 410, 587 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Post-incident analysis involves conducting analysis on the incident and response actions for future reference. It helps to gain a better understanding of the system’s threats and vulnerabilities so that more effective safeguards can be put in place.", "bbox": [ 184, 609, 862, 661 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "Examples of aspects of analysis include:", "bbox": [ 186, 682, 521, 700 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Recommended actions to prevent further attack.", "bbox": [ 191, 724, 618, 740 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Information that is needed quickly and the way to get the information.", "bbox": [ 191, 745, 796, 762 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Additional tools used or needed to aid in the detection and eradication process.", "bbox": [ 191, 765, 865, 782 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Sufficiency in respect of preparation and response.", "bbox": [ 191, 787, 640, 803 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Adequacy in communication.", "bbox": [ 191, 808, 468, 824 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Practical difficulties.", "bbox": [ 191, 828, 398, 845 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "page_number", "text": "47", "bbox": [ 852, 942, 877, 957 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "header", "text": "Post-Incident Actions", "bbox": [ 697, 57, 880, 72 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "footer", "text": "Practice Guide for Information Security Incident Handling", "bbox": [ 115, 941, 594, 959 ], "page_idx": 51 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Damage of incident, which may include:", "bbox": [ 191, 89, 559, 107 ], "page_idx": 52 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(i) Manpower costs required to deal with the incident.", "bbox": [ 220, 110, 687, 128 ], "page_idx": 52 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(ii) Monetary cost.", "bbox": [ 221, 129, 400, 147 ], "page_idx": 52 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(iii) Cost of operation disruption.", "bbox": [ 221, 149, 510, 167 ], "page_idx": 52 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(iv) Value of data, software and hardware lost or damaged, including sensitive data disclosed.", "bbox": [ 221, 170, 877, 203 ], "page_idx": 52 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(v) Legal liability of entrusted confidential data.", "bbox": [ 221, 205, 636, 224 ], "page_idx": 52 }, { "type": "text", "text": "(vi) Public embarrassment or loss of goodwill.", "bbox": [ 221, 227, 618, 243 ], "page_idx": 52 }, { "type": "text", "text": "• Other experiences learnt.", "bbox": [ 191, 248, 431, 265 ], "page_idx": 52 }, { "type": "text", "text": "The analysis should be incorporated into the IT security risk management and continuous improvement processes to strengthen the security protection of the B/D and reduce the chance of an incident.", "bbox": [ 184, 286, 865, 338 ], "page_idx": 52 }, { "type": "text", "text": "10.2 Post-Incident Report", "text_level": 2,
